extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations (public relations educators, agency practitioners, corporate communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the four models of public relations (press agentry/publicity, public information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric), including how and when to use research, press-release/handout practices, and ethical/open communication norms. Useful for deciding model, planning research, and preparing press materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research as a component of public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Research is an important component of modern public relations, but only practitioners whose behaviors fit the two-way asymmetric or two-way symmetric models use research as an important component of their work. Press agents/publicists seldom use research, and public-information specialists do little research beyond occasional readability or readership tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which model a practitioner fits by looking at whether and what kind of research is used. Expect little systematic research from press agentry and public-information models; two-way models rely on research heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative research helps to plan an activity and to choose objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formative research to learn what publics will accept and tolerate (asymmetric model) or to learn how the public perceives the organization and the consequences the organization has for the public (symmetric model). Formative research informs selection of communication objectives and can reveal how well publics understand management and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative research finds out whether the objective has been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct evaluative research to measure attitudes and behavior before and after the public relations effort (thermostat metaphor). In the symmetric model, evaluative research should measure whether understanding between publics and management has improved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of research in the two-way asymmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: In the asymmetric model, practitioners use formative research to find out what the public will accept and tolerate and then identify and promote policies and procedures that the public likes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research is used instrumentally to craft persuasive messages (e.g., determine product features consumers like, then emphasize those features in PR materials). Evaluative research measures campaign effects on attitudes/behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of research in the two-way symmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: In the two-way symmetric model, formative research is used to learn how the public perceives the organization and to determine what consequences the organization has for the public; that information is used to counsel management and possibly change policies to better serve the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use research to inform mutual understanding and policy change; evaluative research should assess improvements in reciprocal understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability tests and readership studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-information specialists may do readability tests to see if information is at the appropriate level and readership studies to see if the audience actually uses the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply readability testing to ensure materials match audience comprehension; use readership studies to verify materials are reaching and used by intended publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal behavioral metrics ('count the house')
rubrics_metrics.description: Press agents/publicists may use informal observation—such as 'count the house'—to see if publicity has resulted in attendance at an event or increased product/service purchases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this as a common, less-rigorous evaluative practice in press agentry; it's a behavioral proxy rather than systematic evaluative research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness and accuracy in press materials (Declaration of Principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ivy Lee's Declaration of Principles: 'This is not a secret press bureau. All our work is done in the open. We aim to supply news. This is not an advertising agency... Our matter is accurate. Further details on any subject treated will be supplied promptly... full information will be given to any editor concerning those on whose behalf an article is sent out... I send out only matter every detail of which I am willing to assist any editor in verifying for himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases/handouts should be openly attributed, accurate, and only contain matter the sender is willing to have verified. Mark handouts clearly with authorship and client/source; prioritize transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide editors assistance and verifiable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply information and be available to assist any editor in verifying facts; provide full information on the sources and the subjects treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issuing releases or handouts, offer prompt access to additional details and verification; cultivate press relations by enabling journalists to perform their job (providing facts rather than bribing or planting anonymous tips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite reporters to develop their own stories / replace press release with reporter invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some organizations have replaced the press release with invitations to reporters to come in and develop their own story about the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use invitations and access as a tool to encourage independent reporting and to foster more complete, less spin-driven coverage—common in two-way symmetric practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue sessions and stakeholder forums
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations may hold dialogue sessions with reporters, educators, community leaders, or other stakeholders to discuss controversial public issues, allowing both sides to present and learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue/forums to achieve mutual understanding and to learn as much from publics as to inform them; appropriate for two-way symmetric model and community relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical norm: tell the truth and change behavior if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Ivy Lee's public-information ethic: 'Tell the truth'—if the truth is damaging, change the organization's behavior so the truth can be told without fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt openness and corrective action as part of PR practice; this is an ethical standard distinguishing public-information/symmetric approaches from cynical press agentry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-agentry anti-patterns (stunts, planted stories, misinformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Press agents historically used stunts, fabricated stories, anonymous tips, and other tricks to get media exposure; 'There's no such thing as bad publicity' summaries this creed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such tactics as an anti-pattern—they may gain short-term attention but undermine credibility and journalistic trust; modern practice and ethics discourage deception and planted anonymous material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting a model based on organizational context
rubrics_metrics.description: Different models are practiced in different contexts: press agentry/publicity in promotions (sports, theater), public information common in government/nonprofits/education, two-way asymmetric in competitive business/consulting, two-way symmetric often in regulated large firms and some consultancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the practice model aligned with organizational goals, regulatory environment, and audience expectations; understand that many practitioners default to public-information, while symmetric practice is less widely adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner role vis-à-vis client and public
rubrics_metrics.description: The public-relations practitioner interprets the organization to the public and the public to the organization; like a lawyer, a practitioner may represent client interests within limits, sometimes without questioning motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of tensions between client advocacy and public interest; the practitioner's role may include counseling management on potential conflicts with public opinion and advising on behavior change when necessary.
